sentences.text: Arcovenator is the only known species in its genus, Arcovenator escotae, a theropod dinosaur belonging to the family Abelisauridae. This animal is characterized by short, high skulls with sculpted surfaces, drastically reduced forelimbs, and robust hind limbs typical of its group.
The name Arcovenator combines the Latin word for hunter with the name of the river Arc, near where the fossils were first discovered.
While the nearly complete skull initially suggested a length of 5 to 6 meters, later estimates in 2016 revised this size to 4.8 meters.
A unique diagnostic trait of the skull roof is a central foramen, an opening that likely housed the pineal gland, situated on a small dome formed by the moderately thick frontal bone.
Ridges on the parietal bones of the skull fuse together to form a sagittal crest running along the midline.
A single maxilla found at Pourcieux is likely referable to Arcovenator based on its proximity in time and space and phylogenetic analysis.
The genus Arcovenator was named by Tortosa and colleagues in 2013, followed by the naming of the species Arcovenator escotae in the same year.
Fossils were discovered near Pourrières in southeastern France during pre-construction surveys for the A8 motorway.

The holotype, the specimen the species is based on, consists of a braincase, skull fragments, a tooth, a tail vertebra, a tibia, and a fibula found together in fluvial sandstone layers characteristic of a river mouth or lobe deposit.
The animal inhabited the Ibero-Armorican island, a large landmass comprising parts of modern-day France, Spain, and Portugal.
The environment featured warm, subhumid climates with marked seasons, where rivers flowed into a perennial lake.
Fossils were found in fluvial sandstone alongside hybodonts, turtles, crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs, sauropods, the ornithopod Rhabdodon, and nodosaurids.
The abundance of fragmentary remains, especially teeth, suggests that medium-sized abelisaurids like Arcovenator were relatively common in the landscape.
Arcovenator lived between 72 and 76 million years ago in the Aix-en-Provence Basin of southeastern France, while other sources place it between 74 and 72 million years ago.
The animal lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages, from 83.6 to 66 million years ago, though other sources place it between 74 and 72 million years ago.
It is debated how European abelisaurs arrived in Europe, with vicariance suggested for older lineages and oceanic dispersal likely for the more recent derived lineage including Arcovenator.
